issues.legal_issue: The absence of a right for a displaced tenant to return after demolition and reconstruction, when a right to return after repairs is provided, does not create an unreasonable classification.
material_facts: The challenged scheme allowed a tenant displaced for repairs to return after the repairs were completed, but did not provide a corresponding right after demolition and reconstruction.
Repairs could generally be completed within a few months, whereas reconstruction could take years, during which a displaced tenant would be expected to find other suitable accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The different treatment of tenants displaced for repairs and those displaced for demolition and reconstruction is rational and does not violate the guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a classification is valid if it has a rational basis; the absence of a right to return after reconstruction does not by itself make a rent-control scheme unfair or unconstitutional. The Court relied on sections 14(1)(a), 14(1)(b), 14(2)(a), 14(2)(b), and 15 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, and applied the principles in State of Madhya Pradesh v. G.C. Mandawar and the decisions concerning the scheme of those provisions, including Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory v. Subbash Chandra Yograj Sinha.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_law: A party challenged the constitutionality of a rent-control law in court.
predicates.repairs_allow_return: The law allows a tenant displaced for repairs to return to the premises after the repairs are completed.
predicates.reconstruction_takes_substantially_longe: Reconstruction is expected to take substantially longer than repairs, so the displaced tenant is expected to find other accommodation.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a rent law that allows return after repairs but reconstruction takes substantially longer, the different return rights are constitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A difference between one state's rent-control law and the laws of other states does not, by itself, establish an equality violation.
material_facts: The challengers relied on the fact that rent-control laws in several other states provided for tenants to return to premises after reconstruction, while the challenged law did not.
issues.conclusion: The difference between the challenged law and rent laws enacted by other states does not by itself make the challenged law unconstitutional under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not permit a law of one state to be struck down merely because it differs from a law on the same subject enacted by another state; the Court relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. G.C. Mandawar.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_law: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law enacted by a state.
predicates.challenged_law_differs_from_other_states: The challenged law differs from laws on the same subject enacted by other states.

issues.definition: When a state law is challenged because it differs from other states' laws, that difference alone does not invalidate it.

issues.legal_issue: A limited exemption from rent-control protections for a building reconstructed after eviction for demolition and rebuilding is not unconstitutional merely because the displaced tenant cannot return to it.
material_facts: The law exempted a new building erected after the original building was demolished from rent-control provisions for a limited period.
The exemption was intended to encourage landlords to replace dilapidated, uneconomic buildings with new accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The limited exemption for a reconstructed building is not discriminatory or unreasonable and does not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature may provide a limited exemption from rent control to encourage construction and increase available accommodation, provided the measure is not otherwise unreasonable or arbitrary. The Court relied on section 16(2) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, and the principles in Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government, Mohinder Kumar v. State of Haryana, and Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_law: A party challenged the constitutionality of a rent-control law in court.
predicates.reconstructed_building_is_exempt_for_lim: The law exempts a building reconstructed after demolition from rent-control restrictions for a limited period.
predicates.exemption_encourages_additional_housing: The exemption is intended to encourage construction that adds accommodation.

issues.definition: A limited exemption for a reconstructed building is constitutional when it is challenged under a rent law and is intended to encourage additional accommodation.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord's ability to seek eviction for demolition and reconstruction is not arbitrary or excessive when the landlord must establish a bona fide requirement before a rent-control authority.
material_facts: The law permitted eviction for demolition and reconstruction only if the landlord bona fide required the building for the immediate purpose of demolition and intended to erect a new building on the site.

A rent-control authority had to assess the bona fides of the claim, considering relevant circumstances such as the building's condition, age, location, the landlord's means, steps toward reconstruction, and the prospects for more profitable use.
The eviction decision was subject to statutory appeal and revision.
issues.conclusion: The demolition-and-reconstruction ground does not confer arbitrary or excessive power on landlords, and the provision is not unconstitutional on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The requirement of bona fide need, assessed by the rent-control authority in light of the totality of relevant circumstances, supplies safeguards against a pretextual eviction claim. The Court relied on section 14(1)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, and on Mehsin Bhai v. Hale and Company, Neta Ram v. Jiwan Lal, Metalware & Co. v. Bansilal Sharma, and Panchamal Narayan Shenoy v. Basthi Venkatesha Shenoy.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_eviction_gro: A party challenged the constitutionality of a legal ground for eviction.
predicates.landlord_claims_demolition_and_reconstru: A landlord seeks eviction to demolish a building and erect a new building on its site.
predicates.decision_maker_assesses_bona_fide_need: The decision-maker evaluates whether the landlord's need is genuine by considering relevant circumstances.

issues.definition: When a challenged eviction ground concerns demolition and reconstruction and the decision-maker assesses the landlord's genuine need, the ground is not arbitrary.
